An Indian soldier stands guard on an armoured vehicle, near the site of a gun battle in Zanglapora, about 65km (40 miles) south of Srinagar, in Indian-administered Kashmir, Wednesday, November 18, 2026 [Dar Yasin/AP Photo]By Muheet Ul IslamPublished On 28 Nov 202628 Nov 2026
Kulgam and Srinagar, Indian-administered Kashmir – After a seven-day search, Indian security forces trapped Mohammad Lateef Bhat in a mosque in Zangalpora village, in Indian-administered Kashmir’s Kulgam district.
A gunfight broke out and Bhat was killed on November 18. Described as a commander of the Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT), a Pakistan-based armed group, Bhat was accused of having shot at soldiers of India’s Central Reserve Police Force a week earlier with another fighter. Three soldiers were injured. His associate was also killed in the days after that attack.
But it was Bhat’s death that grabbed national headlines.
Indian Home Minister Amit Shah, the country’s second-most powerful person after Prime Minister Narendra Modi, told a public gathering that Bhat had been the last local armed fighter before he was killed.
“This development marks a significant change in the security situation in the [Kashmir] valley. It is a matter of pride for us,” Shah said. “No Kashmiri youth is currently involved in terrorist activities in the valley.”
Jammu and Kashmir police also claimed that it was the first time since the armed rebellion against Indian rule in Kashmir began in 1989 that the LeT had no local fighters.

item.title: [BBC World] Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
A Peruvian military helicopter crashed during a rescue missionByJessica LambPublished27 minutes ago
Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.
Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.
Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.
The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.
In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".
It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".
The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.
No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.
Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".
In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.
Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine, according to the United Nations.

item.title: [BBC World] Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Cafer Mahiroğlu says Halk TV has been "destroyed" by Turkish authoritiesByHarry SekulichPublished33 minutes ago
Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.
Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.
Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.
In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.
Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.
Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.
"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.
The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his administration.
The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.
Erdoğan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.

item.title: [BBC China] Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidentsByKelly NgPublished5 hours ago
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."
It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.
But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".
Image source, Dolkun IsaImage caption,
Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades
Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

item.title: [ABC News World] Prosecutors ask for 25 years for man who sold products used by 93 to kill themselves
item.description:
Prosecutors ask for 25 years for man who sold products used by 93 to kill themselves
Prosecutors sought a 25-year prison sentence for a Canadian man who sold products online knowing buyers were likely to use them to kill themselvesByThe Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 4:13 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
NEWMARKET, Ontario -- Ontario prosecutors on Friday sought a 25-year prison sentence for a Canadian man who pleaded guilty to aiding 14 suicides after selling products online knowing buyers were likely to use them to kill themselves.
Kenneth Law, 61, apologized to victims’ families from the prisoner’s box, saying that his actions were “categorically wrong” and promising never to repeat them.
Prosecutors argued that Law was motivated by money. His lawyers sought a 12-year sentence, describing him as a misguided believer in the right to die rather than a “mercenary predator.” A sentencing decision is expected in February.
Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of counseling or aiding suicide involving people in Ontario. The judge is also considering the deaths of 79 people in the United Kingdom.
At a hearing in September, families of people who died after buying lethal products from Law described their lives shattered by grief. Police said Law sold sodium nitrite, a substance commonly used to cure meats that can be deadly if ingested.

item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Pedro Sánchez accused his opponents of hurling insults and lies but his conservative rival has promised a new era of politicsByNick Beake, Europe correspondent, Reporting fromValencia and Paul Kirby, Europe digital editorPublished27 November 2026
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.
Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Alberto Núñez Feijóo's PP holds a narrow lead in the opinion polls
The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.
Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.
Image source, ReutersImage caption,

item.title: [ABC News World] UN rapporteur Albanese in limbo at airport after being denied entry to Costa Rica
item.description:
UN rapporteur Albanese in limbo at airport after being denied entry to Costa Rica
Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories, is stranded at Costa Rica’s main airport awaiting for a court to decide whether she could enter the country after immigration authorities blocked h...ByJAVIER CÓRDOBA Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 1:38 PM
SAN JOSÉ, Costa Rica -- Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian territories, was stranded in an airport terminal on Friday after being denied entry to Costa Rica.
Albanese posted a photo on X showing a suitcase beside a row of empty seats, with the caption: “This is where I will spend my first night in Costa Rica.”
She is awaiting a court decision on whether she can enter the country or must leave.
Costa Rican immigration authorities blocked her entry on Thursday, saying she was the subject of an international “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism and that her presence posed a national security risk.
Albanese is a high-profile independent investigator scrutinizing human rights abuses in the Palestinian territories. She is among a group of experts appointed by the 47-member U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva to monitor and report on human rights conditions in individual countries and the observance of specific rights worldwide.
She was sanctioned by the United States in July 2025 over her work and sharp criticism of U.S. and Israeli policies during the war in Gaza. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described her actions as a “campaign of political and economic warfare against the United States and Israel.”
Albanese had traveled to Costa Rica at the invitation of the University of Costa Rica, which was scheduled to award her an honorary doctorate.

item.title: [ABC News World] Mexico files formal complaint to US over DEA tip line
item.description:
Mexico files formal complaint to US over DEA tip line
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum says the country is filing a formal complaint with the U.S. over a Drug Enforcement Agency tip line for anonymous reports about criminals and corrupt Mexican officialsByFABIOLA SÁNCHEZ Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 1:22 PM
Share
MEXICO CITY -- MEXICO CITY (AP) — Mexico filed a formal complaint with the U.S. over a Drug Enforcement Agency tip line for anonymous reports about criminals and corrupt Mexican officials, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday, escalating a fight over a move she called interference in its internal affairs.
“We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination,” she said in her daily news briefing.
The protest comes as U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is pressuring Mexico to intensify its fight against cartels. It's made a public offer to deploy troops on Mexican soil, something Sheinbaum has ruled out.
DEA chief Terry Cole announced on his X account Wednesday that the agency was opening an anonymous tip line to receive information about members and associates of designated terrorist organizations, corrupt officials who support them, criminal networks and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism in Sinaloa.
The northern state is the stronghold of one of Mexico's most powerful cartels, the Sinaloa Cartel, which Washington designated a terrorist organization along with five other Mexican criminal groups. Cole said the agency also plans to open a tip line for the state of Jalisco.
Sheinbaum once again urged Washington to address drug use and combat drug traffickers within its own territory. She also reaffirmed that Mexico would continue working to confront cartels and prevent drugs from reaching the U.S.

Mr So's parents, both in their 80s, were among the 168 people killed in last year's Hong Kong tower-block blaze - the deadliest the city had seen in decades.
Their building was the first of the Wang Fuk Court complex to catch fire, and their bodies were burned beyond recognition.
In this video Mr So, who is only using his surname, visits his parents' grave and shows what is left of his parents' possessions.

Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blazeByGrace Tsoi, BBC World Service, Phoebe Kong, BBC Chinese , Reporting fromHong Kong and Yvette TanPublished25 November 2026
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.
At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.
It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.
"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.
When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.
She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.
Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.
It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.
"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.
She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.
